1	---
2	name: skill-creator
3	description: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
4	---
5	
6	# Skill Creator
7	
8	A skill for creating new skills and iteratively improving them.
9	
10	At a high level, the process of creating a skill goes like this:
11	
12	- Decide what you want the skill to do and roughly how it should do it
13	- Write a draft of the skill
14	- Create a few test prompts and run claude-with-access-to-the-skill on them
15	- Help the user evaluate the results both qualitatively and quantitatively
16	  - While the runs happen in the background, draft some quantitative evals if there aren't any (if there are some, you can either use as is or modify if you feel something needs to change about them). Then explain them to the user (or if they already existed, explain the ones that already exist)
17	  - Use the `eval-viewer/generate_review.py` script to show the user the results for them to look at, and also let them look at the quantitative metrics
18	- Rewrite the skill based on feedback from the user's evaluation of the results (and also if there are any glaring flaws that become apparent from the quantitative benchmarks)
19	- Repeat until you're satisfied
20	- Expand the test set and try again at larger scale
21	
22	Your job when using this skill is to figure out where the user is in this process and then jump in and help them progress through these stages. So for instance, maybe they're like "I want to make a skill for X". You can help narrow down what they mean, write a draft, write the test cases, figure out how they want to evaluate, run all the prompts, and repeat.
23	
24	On the other hand, maybe they already have a draft of the skill. In this case you can go straight to the eval/iterate part of the loop.
25	
26	Of course, you should always be flexible and if the user is like "I don't need to run a bunch of evaluations, just vibe with me", you can do that instead.
27	
28	Then after the skill is done (but again, the order is flexible), you can also run the skill description improver, which we have a whole separate script for, to optimize the triggering of the skill.
29	
30	Cool? Cool.
31	
32	## Communicating with the user
33	
34	The skill creator is liable to be used by people across a wide range of familiarity with coding jargon. If you haven't heard (and how could you, it's only very recently that it started), there's a trend now where the power of Claude is inspiring plumbers to open up their terminals, parents and grandparents to google "how to install npm". On the other hand, the bulk of users are probably fairly computer-literate.
35	
36	So please pay attention to context cues to understand how to phrase your communication! In the default case, just to give you some idea:
37	
38	- "evaluation" and "benchmark" are borderline, but OK
39	- for "JSON" and "assertion" you want to see serious cues from the user that they know what those things are before using them without explaining them
40	
41	It's OK to briefly explain terms if you're in doubt, and feel free to clarify terms with a short definition if you're unsure if the user will get it.
42	
43	---
44	
45	## Creating a skill
46	
47	### Capture Intent
48	
49	Start by understanding the user's intent. The current conversation might already contain a workflow the user wants to capture (e.g., they say "turn this into a skill"). If so, extract answers from the conversation history first — the tools used, the sequence of steps, corrections the user made, input/output formats observed. The user may need to fill the gaps, and should confirm before proceeding to the next step.
50	
51	1. What should this skill enable Claude to do?
52	2. When should this skill trigger? (what user phrases/contexts)
53	3. What's the expected output format?
54	4. Should we set up test cases to verify the skill works? Skills with objectively verifiable outputs (file transforms, data extraction, code generation, fixed workflow steps) benefit from test cases. Skills with subjective outputs (writing style, art) often don't need them. Suggest the appropriate default based on the skill type, but let the user decide.
55	
56	### Interview and Research
57	
58	Proactively ask questions about edge cases, input/output formats, example files, success criteria, and dependencies. Wait to write test prompts until you've got this part ironed out.
59	
60	Check available MCPs - if useful for research (searching docs, finding similar skills, looking up best practices), research in parallel via subagents if available, otherwise inline. Come prepared with context to reduce burden on the user.
61	
62	### Write the SKILL.md
63	
64	Based on the user interview, fill in these components:
65	
66	- **name**: Skill identifier
67	- **description**: When to trigger, what it does. This is the primary triggering mechanism - include both what the skill does AND specific contexts for when to use it. All "when to use" info goes here, not in the body. Note: currently Claude has a tendency to "undertrigger" skills -- to not use them when they'd be useful. To combat this, please make the skill descriptions a little bit "pushy". So for instance, instead of "How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data.", you might write "How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data. Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions dashboards, data visualization, internal metrics, or wants to display any kind of company data, even if they don't explicitly ask for a 'dashboard.'"
68	- **compatibility**: Required tools, dependencies (optional, rarely needed)
69	- **the rest of the skill :)**
70	
71	### Skill Writing Guide
72	
73	#### Anatomy of a Skill
74	
75	```
76	skill-name/
77	├── SKILL.md (required)
78	│   ├── YAML frontmatter (name, description required)
79	│   └── Markdown instructions
80	└── Bundled Resources (optional)
81	    ├── scripts/    - Executable code for deterministic/repetitive tasks
82	    ├── references/ - Docs loaded into context as needed
83	    └── assets/     - Files used in output (templates, icons, fonts)
84	```
85	
86	#### Progressive Disclosure
87	
88	Skills use a three-level loading system:
89	1. **Metadata** (name + description) - Always in context (~100 words)
90	2. **SKILL.md body** - In context whenever skill triggers (<500 lines ideal)
91	3. **Bundled resources** - As needed (unlimited, scripts can execute without loading)
92	
93	These word counts are approximate and you can feel free to go longer if needed.
94	
95	**Key patterns:**
96	- Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines; if you're approaching this limit, add an additional layer of hierarchy along with clear pointers about where the model using the skill should go next to follow up.
97	- Reference files clearly from SKILL.md with guidance on when to read them
98	- For large reference files (>300 lines), include a table of contents
99	
100	**Domain organization**: When a skill supports multiple domains/frameworks, organize by variant:
101	```
102	cloud-deploy/
103	├── SKILL.md (workflow + selection)
104	└── references/
105	    ├── aws.md
106	    ├── gcp.md
107	    └── azure.md
108	```
109	Claude reads only the relevant reference file.
110	
111	#### Principle of Lack of Surprise
112	
113	This goes without saying, but skills must not contain malware, exploit code, or any content that could compromise system security. A skill's contents should not surprise the user in their intent if described. Don't go along with requests to create misleading skills or skills designed to facilitate unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or other malicious activities. Things like a "roleplay as an XYZ" are OK though.
114	
115	#### Writing Patterns
116	
117	Prefer using the imperative form in instructions.
118	
119	**Defining output formats** - You can do it like this:
120	```markdown
121	## Report structure
122	ALWAYS use this exact template:
123	# [Title]
124	## Executive summary
125	## Key findings
126	## Recommendations
127	```
128	
129	**Examples pattern** - It's useful to include examples. You can format them like this (but if "Input" and "Output" are in the examples you might want to deviate a little):
130	```markdown
131	## Commit message format
132	**Example 1:**
133	Input: Added user authentication with JWT tokens
134	Output: feat(auth): implement JWT-based authentication
135	```
136	
137	### Writing Style
138	
139	Try to explain to the model why things are important in lieu of heavy-handed musty MUSTs. Use theory of mind and try to make the skill general and not super-narrow to specific examples. Start by writing a draft and then look at it with fresh eyes and improve it.
140	
141	### Test Cases
142	
143	After writing the skill draft, come up with 2-3 realistic test prompts — the kind of thing a real user would actually say. Share them with the user: [you don't have to use this exact language] "Here are a few test cases I'd like to try. Do these look right, or do you want to add more?" Then run them.
144	
145	Save test cases to `evals/evals.json`. Don't write assertions yet — just the prompts. You'll draft assertions in the next step while the runs are in progress.
146	
147	```json
148	{
149	  "skill_name": "example-skill",
150	  "evals": [
151	    {
152	      "id": 1,
153	      "prompt": "User's task prompt",
154	      "expected_output": "Description of expected result",
155	      "files": []
156	    }
157	  ]
158	}
159	```
160	
161	See `references/schemas.md` for the full schema (including the `assertions` field, which you'll add later).
162	
163	## Running and evaluating test cases
164	
165	This section is one continuous sequence — don't stop partway through. Do NOT use `/skill-test` or any other testing skill.
166	
167	Put results in `<skill-name>-workspace/` as a sibling to the skill directory. Within the workspace, organize results by iteration (`iteration-1/`, `iteration-2/`, etc.) and within that, each test case gets a directory (`eval-0/`, `eval-1/`, etc.). Don't create all of this upfront — just create directories as you go.
168	
169	### Step 1: Spawn all runs (with-skill AND baseline) in the same turn
170	
171	For each test case, spawn two subagents in the same turn — one with the skill, one without. This is important: don't spawn the with-skill runs first and then come back for baselines later. Launch everything at once so it all finishes around the same time.
172	
173	**With-skill run:**
174	
175	```
176	Execute this task:
177	- Skill path: <path-to-skill>
178	- Task: <eval prompt>
179	- Input files: <eval files if any, or "none">
180	- Save outputs to: <workspace>/iteration-<N>/eval-<ID>/with_skill/outputs/
181	- Outputs to save: <what the user cares about — e.g., "the .docx file", "the final CSV">
182	```
183	
184	**Baseline run** (same prompt, but the baseline depends on context):
185	- **Creating a new skill**: no skill at all. Same prompt, no skill path, save to `without_skill/outputs/`.
186	- **Improving an existing skill**: the old version. Before editing, snapshot the skill (`cp -r <skill-path> <workspace>/skill-snapshot/`), then point the baseline subagent at the snapshot. Save to `old_skill/outputs/`.
187	
188	Write an `eval_metadata.json` for each test case (assertions can be empty for now). Give each eval a descriptive name based on what it's testing — not just "eval-0". Use this name for the directory too. If this iteration uses new or modified eval prompts, create these files for each new eval directory — don't assume they carry over from previous iterations.
189	
190	```json
191	{
192	  "eval_id": 0,
193	  "eval_name": "descriptive-name-here",
194	  "prompt": "The user's task prompt",
195	  "assertions": []
196	}
197	```
198	
199	### Step 2: While runs are in progress, draft assertions
200	
201	Don't just wait for the runs to finish — you can use this time productively. Draft quantitative assertions for each test case and explain them to the user. If assertions already exist in `evals/evals.json`, review them and explain what they check.
202	
203	Good assertions are objectively verifiable and have descriptive names — they should read clearly in the benchmark viewer so someone glancing at the results immediately understands what each one checks. Subjective skills (writing style, design quality) are better evaluated qualitatively — don't force assertions onto things that need human judgment.
204	
205	Update the `eval_metadata.json` files and `evals/evals.json` with the assertions once drafted. Also explain to the user what they'll see in the viewer — both the qualitative outputs and the quantitative benchmark.
206	
207	### Step 3: As runs complete, capture timing data
208	
209	When each subagent task completes, you receive a notification containing `total_tokens` and `duration_ms`. Save this data immediately to `timing.json` in the run directory:
210	
211	```json
212	{
213	  "total_tokens": 84852,
214	  "duration_ms": 23332,
215	  "total_duration_seconds": 23.3
216	}
217	```
218	
219	This is the only opportunity to capture this data — it comes through the task notification and isn't persisted elsewhere. Process each notification as it arrives rather than trying to batch them.
220	
221	### Step 4: Grade, aggregate, and launch the viewer
222	
223	Once all runs are done:
224	
225	1. **Grade each run** — spawn a grader subagent (or grade inline) that reads `agents/grader.md` and evaluates each assertion against the outputs. Save results to `grading.json` in each run directory. The grading.json expectations array must use the fields `text`, `passed`, and `evidence` (not `name`/`met`/`details` or other variants) — the viewer depends on these exact field names. For assertions that can be checked programmatically, write and run a script rather than eyeballing it — scripts are faster, more reliable, and can be reused across iterations.
226	
227	2. **Aggregate into benchmark** — run the aggregation script from the skill-creator directory:
228	   ```bash
229	   python -m scripts.aggregate_benchmark <workspace>/iteration-N --skill-name <name>
230	   ```
231	   This produces `benchmark.json` and `benchmark.md` with pass_rate, time, and tokens for each configuration, with mean ± stddev and the delta. If generating benchmark.json manually, see `references/schemas.md` for the exact schema the viewer expects.
232	Put each with_skill version before its baseline counterpart.
233	
234	3. **Do an analyst pass** — read the benchmark data and surface patterns the aggregate stats might hide. See `agents/analyzer.md` (the "Analyzing Benchmark Results" section) for what to look for — things like assertions that always pass regardless of skill (non-discriminating), high-variance evals (possibly flaky), and time/token tradeoffs.
235	
236	4. **Launch the viewer** with both qualitative outputs and quantitative data:
237	   ```bash
238	   nohup python <skill-creator-path>/eval-viewer/generate_review.py \
239	     <workspace>/iteration-N \
240	     --skill-name "my-skill" \
241	     --benchmark <workspace>/iteration-N/benchmark.json \
242	     > /dev/null 2>&1 &
243	   VIEWER_PID=$!
244	   ```
245	   For iteration 2+, also pass `--previous-workspace <workspace>/iteration-<N-1>`.
246	
247	   **Cowork / headless environments:** If `webbrowser.open()` is not available or the environment has no display, use `--static <output_path>` to write a standalone HTML file instead of starting a server. Feedback will be downloaded as a `feedback.json` file when the user clicks "Submit All Reviews". After download, copy `feedback.json` into the workspace directory for the next iteration to pick up.
248	
249	Note: please use generate_review.py to create the viewer; there's no need to write custom HTML.
250	
251	5. **Tell the user** something like: "I've opened the results in your browser. There are two tabs — 'Outputs' lets you click through each test case and leave feedback, 'Benchmark' shows the quantitative comparison. When you're done, come back here and let me know."
252	
253	### What the user sees in the viewer
254	
255	The "Outputs" tab shows one test case at a time:
256	- **Prompt**: the task that was given
257	- **Output**: the files the skill produced, rendered inline where possible
258	- **Previous Output** (iteration 2+): collapsed section showing last iteration's output
259	- **Formal Grades** (if grading was run): collapsed section showing assertion pass/fail
260	- **Feedback**: a textbox that auto-saves as they type
261	- **Previous Feedback** (iteration 2+): their comments from last time, shown below the textbox
262	
263	The "Benchmark" tab shows the stats summary: pass rates, timing, and token usage for each configuration, with per-eval breakdowns and analyst observations.
264	
265	Navigation is via prev/next buttons or arrow keys. When done, they click "Submit All Reviews" which saves all feedback to `feedback.json`.
266	
267	### Step 5: Read the feedback
268	
269	When the user tells you they're done, read `feedback.json`:
270	
271	```json
272	{
273	  "reviews": [
274	    {"run_id": "eval-0-with_skill", "feedback": "the chart is missing axis labels", "timestamp": "..."},
275	    {"run_id": "eval-1-with_skill", "feedback": "", "timestamp": "..."},
276	    {"run_id": "eval-2-with_skill", "feedback": "perfect, love this", "timestamp": "..."}
277	  ],
278	  "status": "complete"
279	}
280	```
281	
282	Empty feedback means the user thought it was fine. Focus your improvements on the test cases where the user had specific complaints.
283	
284	Kill the viewer server when you're done with it:
285	
286	```bash
287	kill $VIEWER_PID 2>/dev/null
288	```
289	
290	---
291	
292	## Improving the skill
293	
294	This is the heart of the loop. You've run the test cases, the user has reviewed the results, and now you need to make the skill better based on their feedback.
295	
296	### How to think about improvements
297	
298	1. **Generalize from the feedback.** The big picture thing that's happening here is that we're trying to create skills that can be used a million times (maybe literally, maybe even more who knows) across many different prompts. Here you and the user are iterating on only a few examples over and over again because it helps move faster. The user knows these examples in and out and it's quick for them to assess new outputs. But if the skill you and the user are codeveloping works only for those examples, it's useless. Rather than put in fiddly overfitty changes, or oppressively constrictive MUSTs, if there's some stubborn issue, you might try branching out and using different metaphors, or recommending different patterns of working. It's relatively cheap to try and maybe you'll land on something great.
299	
300	2. **Keep the prompt lean.** Remove things that aren't pulling their weight. Make sure to read the transcripts, not just the final outputs — if it looks like the skill is making the model waste a bunch of time doing things that are unproductive, you can try getting rid of the parts of the skill that are making it do that and seeing what happens.
301	
302	3. **Explain the why.** Try hard to explain the **why** behind everything you're asking the model to do. Today's LLMs are *smart*. They have good theory of mind and when given a good harness can go beyond rote instructions and really make things happen. Even if the feedback from the user is terse or frustrated, try to actually understand the task and why the user is writing what they wrote, and what they actually wrote, and then transmit this understanding into the instructions. If you find yourself writing ALWAYS or NEVER in all caps, or using super rigid structures, that's a yellow flag — if possible, reframe and explain the reasoning so that the model understands why the thing you're asking for is important. That's a more humane, powerful, and effective approach.
303	
304	4. **Look for repeated work across test cases.** Read the transcripts from the test runs and notice if the subagents all independently wrote similar helper scripts or took the same multi-step approach to something. If all 3 test cases resulted in the subagent writing a `create_docx.py` or a `build_chart.py`, that's a strong signal the skill should bundle that script. Write it once, put it in `scripts/`, and tell the skill to use it. This saves every future invocation from reinventing the wheel.
305	
306	This task is pretty important (we are trying to create billions a year in economic value here!) and your thinking time is not the blocker; take your time and really mull things over. I'd suggest writing a draft revision and then looking at it anew and making improvements. Really do your best to get into the head of the user and understand what they want and need.
307	
308	### The iteration loop
309	
310	After improving the skill:
311	
312	1. Apply your improvements to the skill
313	2. Rerun all test cases into a new `iteration-<N+1>/` directory, including baseline runs. If you're creating a new skill, the baseline is always `without_skill` (no skill) — that stays the same across iterations. If you're improving an existing skill, use your judgment on what makes sense as the baseline: the original version the user came in with, or the previous iteration.
314	3. Launch the reviewer with `--previous-workspace` pointing at the previous iteration
315	4. Wait for the user to review and tell you they're done
316	5. Read the new feedback, improve again, repeat
317	
318	Keep going until:
319	- The user says they're happy
320	- The feedback is all empty (everything looks good)
321	- You're not making meaningful progress
322	
323	---
324	
325	## Advanced: Blind comparison
326	
327	For situations where you want a more rigorous comparison between two versions of a skill (e.g., the user asks "is the new version actually better?"), there's a blind comparison system. Read `agents/comparator.md` and `agents/analyzer.md` for the details. The basic idea is: give two outputs to an independent agent without telling it which is which, and let it judge quality. Then analyze why the winner won.
328	
329	This is optional, requires subagents, and most users won't need it. The human review loop is usually sufficient.
330	
331	---
332	
333	## Description Optimization
334	
335	The description field in SKILL.md frontmatter is the primary mechanism that determines whether Claude invokes a skill. After creating or improving a skill, offer to optimize the description for better triggering accuracy.
336	
337	### Step 1: Generate trigger eval queries
338	
339	Create 20 eval queries — a mix of should-trigger and should-not-trigger. Save as JSON:
340	
341	```json
342	[
343	  {"query": "the user prompt", "should_trigger": true},
344	  {"query": "another prompt", "should_trigger": false}
345	]
346	```
347	
348	The queries must be realistic and something a Claude Code or Claude.ai user would actually type. Not abstract requests, but requests that are concrete and specific and have a good amount of detail. For instance, file paths, personal context about the user's job or situation, column names and values, company names, URLs. A little bit of backstory. Some might be in lowercase or contain abbreviations or typos or casual speech. Use a mix of different lengths, and focus on edge cases rather than making them clear-cut (the user will get a chance to sign off on them).
349	
350	Bad: `"Format this data"`, `"Extract text from PDF"`, `"Create a chart"`
351	
352	Good: `"ok so my boss just sent me this xlsx file (its in my downloads, called something like 'Q4 sales final FINAL v2.xlsx') and she wants me to add a column that shows the profit margin as a percentage. The revenue is in column C and costs are in column D i think"`
353	
354	For the **should-trigger** queries (8-10), think about coverage. You want different phrasings of the same intent — some formal, some casual. Include cases where the user doesn't explicitly name the skill or file type but clearly needs it. Throw in some uncommon use cases and cases where this skill competes with another but should win.
355	
356	For the **should-not-trigger** queries (8-10), the most valuable ones are the near-misses — queries that share keywords or concepts with the skill but actually need something different. Think adjacent domains, ambiguous phrasing where a naive keyword match would trigger but shouldn't, and cases where the query touches on something the skill does but in a context where another tool is more appropriate.
357	
358	The key thing to avoid: don't make should-not-trigger queries obviously irrelevant. "Write a fibonacci function" as a negative test for a PDF skill is too easy — it doesn't test anything. The negative cases should be genuinely tricky.
359	
360	### Step 2: Review with user
361	
362	Present the eval set to the user for review using the HTML template:
363	
364	1. Read the template from `assets/eval_review.html`
365	2. Replace the placeholders:
366	   - `__EVAL_DATA_PLACEHOLDER__` → the JSON array of eval items (no quotes around it — it's a JS variable assignment)
367	   - `__SKILL_NAME_PLACEHOLDER__` → the skill's name
368	   - `__SKILL_DESCRIPTION_PLACEHOLDER__` → the skill's current description
369	3. Write to a temp file (e.g., `/tmp/eval_review_<skill-name>.html`) and open it: `open /tmp/eval_review_<skill-name>.html`
370	4. The user can edit queries, toggle should-trigger, add/remove entries, then click "Export Eval Set"
371	5. The file downloads to `~/Downloads/eval_set.json` — check the Downloads folder for the most recent version in case there are multiple (e.g., `eval_set (1).json`)
372	
373	This step matters — bad eval queries lead to bad descriptions.
374	
375	### Step 3: Run the optimization loop
376	
377	Tell the user: "This will take some time — I'll run the optimization loop in the background and check on it periodically."
378	
379	Save the eval set to the workspace, then run in the background:
380	
381	```bash
382	python -m scripts.run_loop \
383	  --eval-set <path-to-trigger-eval.json> \
384	  --skill-path <path-to-skill> \
385	  --model <model-id-powering-this-session> \
386	  --max-iterations 5 \
387	  --verbose
388	```
389	
390	Use the model ID from your system prompt (the one powering the current session) so the triggering test matches what the user actually experiences.
391	
392	While it runs, periodically tail the output to give the user updates on which iteration it's on and what the scores look like.
393	
394	This handles the full optimization loop automatically. It splits the eval set into 60% train and 40% held-out test, evaluates the current description (running each query 3 times to get a reliable trigger rate), then calls Claude to propose improvements based on what failed. It re-evaluates each new description on both train and test, iterating up to 5 times. When it's done, it opens an HTML report in the browser showing the results per iteration and returns JSON with `best_description` — selected by test score rather than train score to avoid overfitting.
395	
396	### How skill triggering works
397	
398	Understanding the triggering mechanism helps design better eval queries. Skills appear in Claude's `available_skills` list with their name + description, and Claude decides whether to consult a skill based on that description. The important thing to know is that Claude only consults skills for tasks it can't easily handle on its own — simple, one-step queries like "read this PDF" may not trigger a skill even if the description matches perfectly, because Claude can handle them directly with basic tools. Complex, multi-step, or specialized queries reliably trigger skills when the description matches.
399	
400	This means your eval queries should be substantive enough that Claude would actually benefit from consulting a skill. Simple queries like "read file X" are poor test cases — they won't trigger skills regardless of description quality.
401	
402	### Step 4: Apply the result
403	
404	Take `best_description` from the JSON output and update the skill's SKILL.md frontmatter. Show the user before/after and report the scores.
405	
406	---
407	
408	### Package and Present (only if a file-delivery tool is available)
409	
410	Check whether you have access to a tool that presents files to the user — `present_files`, or `SendUserFile` in Cowork remote. If you have neither, skip this step. If you do, package the skill and send the user the resulting `.skill` file with that tool:
411	
412	```bash
413	python -m scripts.package_skill <path/to/skill-folder>
414	```
415	
416	The presented `.skill` (or bare `SKILL.md`) file card shows a **Save skill** button when the user's org allows skill creation; clicking it installs the skill into their profile.
417	
418	---
419	
420	## Claude.ai-specific instructions
421	
422	In Claude.ai, the core workflow is the same (draft → test → review → improve → repeat), but because Claude.ai doesn't have subagents, some mechanics change. Here's what to adapt:
423	
424	**Running test cases**: No subagents means no parallel execution. For each test case, read the skill's SKILL.md, then follow its instructions to accomplish the test prompt yourself. Do them one at a time. This is less rigorous than independent subagents (you wrote the skill and you're also running it, so you have full context), but it's a useful sanity check — and the human review step compensates. Skip the baseline runs — just use the skill to complete the task as requested.
425	
426	**Reviewing results**: If you can't open a browser (e.g., Claude.ai's VM has no display, or you're on a remote server), skip the browser reviewer entirely. If the output is a file the user needs to see (like a .docx or .xlsx), save it to the filesystem and tell them where it is so they can download and inspect it. Ask for feedback inline: "How does this look? Anything you'd change?"
427	
428	**Benchmarking**: Skip the quantitative benchmarking — it relies on baseline comparisons which aren't meaningful without subagents. Focus on qualitative feedback from the user.
429	
430	**The iteration loop**: Same as before — improve the skill, rerun the test cases, ask for feedback — just without the browser reviewer in the middle. You can still organize results into iteration directories on the filesystem if you have one.
431	
432	**Description optimization**: This section requires the `claude` CLI tool (specifically `claude -p`) which is only available in Claude Code. Skip it if you're on Claude.ai.
433	
434	**Blind comparison**: Requires subagents. Skip it.
435	
436	**Packaging**: The `package_skill.py` script works anywhere with Python and a filesystem. On Claude.ai, you can run it and the user can download the resulting `.skill` file.
437	
438	**Updating an existing skill**: The user might be asking you to update an existing skill, not create a new one. In this case:
439	- **Preserve the original name.** Note the skill's directory name and `name` frontmatter field -- use them unchanged. E.g., if the installed skill is `research-helper`, output `research-helper.skill` (not `research-helper-v2`).
440	- **Copy to a writeable location before editing.** The installed skill path may be read-only. Copy to `/tmp/skill-name/`, edit there, and package from the copy.
441	- **If packaging manually, stage in `/tmp/` first**, then copy to the output directory -- direct writes may fail due to permissions.
442	
443	---

Also use it when the user describes a task and mentions Entire, trails, changes, or checkpoints, even without using those words. --- # Entire Trail An Entire **trail** is a project-level work item holding the intent — the *why* of some work. A **change** is one branch in one repo working on that intent. A **checkpoint** is the AI session captured automatically at each commit. A **finding** is structured review feedback attached to a change. This skill takes a task from intent through to a reported trail. ## Read the flags, don't guess them The CLI is the source of truth for its own usage and its flags change between versions. Before running an unfamiliar subcommand, read its flags: ```sh entire agent-help # overview, and which command applies when entire agent-help trail # trail subcommands and shared flags entire agent-help trail # exact flags for one subcommand ``` Add `--json` for structured output — it parses more reliably than the table format, and `trail show --json` is how you see a trail's `changes[]`. ## Selector discipline Users paste URLs; commands take selectors. Map the path after the host: | URL path | Selector | | --- | --- | | `//-/trails/

` | project trail `

` | | `//-/trails/

/changes//` | change `/` | | `///-/trails/

/changes/` | change `/` | | `///trails/` | change `/` | Never pass a URL to a command. Project trails and changes are numbered separately, so passing `

` where a change is expected — or the reverse — targets the wrong thing. When you resolve a pasted URL, say what you resolved it to before acting on it. `--project /` is required for `list`; elsewhere it defaults to the repo's namespace. The repo itself is auto-detected from the git remote, so never ask the user which repo they are in — pass `--repo` only to target a *different* one. ## Workflow ### 1. Find where the work belongs If the user pasted a trail URL, resolve it to a selector and confirm the traal's title and status before acting. Otherwise list what already exists: ```sh entire trail list --project / ``` - One obvious open trail matching the task → use it, and say which you chose. - Several plausible trails → ask which one, rather than guessing. - Nothing matching → this is new work; create a trail. ### 2. Capture the intent The trail's title and body are the durable record of *why* this work exists, so write them for someone who wasn't in the conversation. - **Title** — the outcome, short: `Fix aggregation dropping transcripts`. - **Body** — why it matters and what "done" looks like. - **Type** — `--type feature|bug|task`. ```sh entire trail update

--title "..." --body "..." --type feature ``` A trail's description should stay current: when the goal shifts mid-work, update it rather than letting it drift from reality. ### 3. Attach a change A change is a branch. The base branch (`main`) is not itself a meaningful change — new work needs a branch off it. --branch --base main ``` A branch can only belong to one trail; linking a branch that is already claimed is rejected. Post findings Findings are how review feedback reaches the work. Post them against the change, with the file and line that the finding is about: ```sh entire trail finding add --trail \ --file lib/event_aggregation_pipeline.py --line 50 \ --severity medium -m "What is wrong and why it matters" ``` `--confidence` takes 0.0–1.0, and `--patch` / `--patch-file` attach a suggested diff (it must modify a single existing file in the worktree). Findings are for feedback. Comments (`entire trail comment`) are for people — post review feedback as a finding, not a comment. ### 6. Report Give the user the full URLs of the trail and the change, what was done, and what is still outstanding. Include the URL whenever you reference a trail or change so they can click through. ## Guardrails - `entire trail` commands need network access and the OS keychain. If you hit "Keychain is not accessible" or a network error, that is the sandbox, not a logged-out state: ask to re-run it unsandboxed. Do not run `entire login`. - `enable`, `disable`, `clean`, `auth`, `login`, and `logout` are the user's to run — suggest them, don't run them. - Writing intent onto a shared trail is outward-facing. Confirm the title and body with the user before writing, and confirm before creating a trail. - If it's unclear whether work belongs on an existing trail or a new one, ask rather than picking for them. ## Quick reference | Task | Command | | --- | --- | | List trails | `entire trail list --project /` | | Inspect a trail | `entire trail show

--project / --json` | | Set intent | `entire trail update

--title "..." --body "..."` | | New trail + branch | `entire trail create ... --branch-action=create --base main` | | Attach existing branch | `entire trail link

--branch --base main` | | Get onto a change | `entire trail checkout --trail [--worktree]` | | Post a finding | `entire trail finding add --trail --file -m "..."` | | Checkpoints | `entire checkpoint list` / `entire status` |

# uv Development Workflow

Guidance for working with this project using `uv` as the package manager and
build tool.

## Key Commands

### Install/Sync Dependencies
```sh
uv sync
```
This installs all dependencies (including dev dependencies) as specified in `pyproject.toml`.

### Run Python Commands
```sh
uv run <command>
```
Example:
```sh
uv run pytest
uv run python main.py
uv run ruff check .
```

### Run Tests
```sh
uv run pytest
uv run pytest -v  # verbose mode
uv run pytest tests/  # specific test directory
uv run pytest --cov=lib --cov-report=term-missing  # with coverage
```

### Format Code
```sh
uv run ruff check .
uv run ruff format .
```

### Pre-commit Hooks
```sh
uv run pre-commit run --all-files
```

## Project Structure Notes

- Python 3.12 is required (pinned in `.python-version`)
- `uv` is configured to use the pyenv-managed Python (`python-preference = "only-system"`)
- Tests are located in the `tests/` directory
- Main entry points: `main.py`, `client.py`
- Library code: `lib/` directory

## TLS/Security Note

This project uses pinned versions of `certifi` and `virtualenv` to address the eMudhra/emSign CA certificate incident. Ensure any environments created outside uv maintain `pip >= 26.2.2` and `certifi >= 2026.10.19`.

Built and pushed as `22966fa`. ## What you can now call **`/entire-trail `** — e.g. `/entire-trail fix the aggregation drop`. It runs the full lifecycle: finds or creates the trail, writes the intent, creates and attaches a branch as a change, does the work, posts findings, and reports the URLs. It's also discoverable by description, so it'll surface on things like *"open a trail for this"*, *"attach this branch to the trail"*, *"post findings on this change"*, or a pasted `entire.com` URL. ## The files `.claude/skills/entire-trail/SKILL.md` (165 lines) covers: - **The model** — trail = intent, change = branch, checkpoint = auto-captured AI session, finding = structured feedback. Encoding this matters because it stops the model from conflating the four. - **Selector discipline** — the URL→selector mapping table, plus the rule that project trails and changes are numbered *separately*. This was the sharpest edge in the CLI: passing `

` where a change is expected silently targets the wrong thing. - **The workflow**, with the `main`-isn't-a-change trap written down explicitly (linking the base branch as a change is meaningless — you need a branch off it). - **Guardrails** — the sandbox-vs-logged-out distinction (re-run unsandboxed, never `entire login`), that `enable`/`disable`/`clean`/`auth` are the user's to run, and that writing intent to a shared trail needs confirmation first. ## One thing I fixed along the way Your `uv-workflow` skill was never actually loading. It sat at `.claude/skills/uv-workflow.md` — a flat file with no frontmatter — so Claude Code never registered it. Skills need `/SKILL.md` with `name` and `description` frontmatter. It's now `.claude/skills/uv-workflow/SKILL.md` and confirmed present in the available-skills list, alongside `entire-trail`. ## One thing I couldn't finish I tried to `git rm` the old flat `.claude/skills/uv-workflow.md` and the permission classifier blocked it — deleting a tracked file without you naming it explicitly. It's harmless (it's inert without frontmatter, and it doesn't shadow the new directory), but it's stale duplicate content in the repo. It's still tracked from commit `7525bdb`. Run this to clean it up: ```sh git rm .claude/skills/uv-workflow.md && git commit -m "Remove superseded flat uv-workflow skill" ``` Say the word and I'll run it with your approval. Two notes for when you use the skill: the CLI's `trail link` rejects a branch that already belongs to another trail — the skill tells the model to look up the branch's current trail with `entire trail show --branch ` rather than guess. And `entire trail finding add --patch` only accepts a diff touching a single existing file in the worktree, which is tighter than you'd expect.

Base directory for this skill: /Users/paolo/dev/helper/.claude/skills/entire-trail # Entire Trail An Entire **trail** is a project-level work item holding the intent — the *why* of some work. A **change** is one branch in one repo working on that intent. A **checkpoint** is the AI session captured automatically at each commit. A **finding** is structured review feedback attached to a change. This skill takes a task from intent through to a reported trail. ## Read the flags, don't guess them The CLI is the source of truth for its own usage and its flags change between versions. Before running an unfamiliar subcommand, read its flags: ```sh entire agent-help # overview, and which command applies when entire agent-help trail # trail subcommands and shared flags entire agent-help trail # exact flags for one subcommand ``` Add `--json` for structured output — it parses more reliably than the table format, and `trail show --json` is how you see a trail's `changes[]`. ## Selector discipline Users paste URLs; commands take selectors. Map the path after the host: | URL path | Selector | | --- | --- | | `//-/trails/

` | project trail `

` | | `//-/trails/

/changes//` | change `/` | | `///-/trails/

/changes/` | change `/` | | `///trails/` | change `/` | Never pass a URL to a command. Project trails and changes are numbered separately, so passing `

` where a change is expected — or the reverse — targets the wrong thing. When you resolve a pasted URL, say what you resolved it to before acting on it. `--project /` is required for `list`; elsewhere it defaults to the repo's namespace. The repo itself is auto-detected from the git remote, so never ask the user which repo they are in — pass `--repo` only to target a *different* one. ## Workflow ### 1. Find where the work belongs If the user pasted a trail URL, resolve it to a selector and confirm the traal's title and status before acting. Otherwise list what already exists: ```sh entire trail list --project / ``` - One obvious open trail matching the task → use it, and say which you chose. - Several plausible trails → ask which one, rather than guessing. - Nothing matching → this is new work; create a trail. ### 2. Capture the intent The trail's title and body are the durable record of *why* this work exists, so write them for someone who wasn't in the conversation. - **Title** — the outcome, short: `Fix aggregation dropping transcripts`. - **Body** — why it matters and what "done" looks like. - **Type** — `--type feature|bug|task`. ```sh entire trail update

--title "..." --body "..." --type feature ``` A trail's description should stay current: when the goal shifts mid-work, update it rather than letting it drift from reality. ### 3. Attach a change A change is a branch. The base branch (`main`) is not itself a meaningful change — new work needs a branch off it. New work — creates the branch and attaches it in one step: ```sh entire trail create --project / \ --title "..." --body "..." --type feature \ --branch-action=create --base main ``` Existing branch — `--branch-action` defaults to `link`, which attaches work that already exists: ```sh entire trail link

--branch --base main ``` A branch can only belong to one trail; linking a branch that is already claimed is rejected. When that happens, find its current trail with `entire trail show --branch ` rather than guessing. To get back onto a change later, `entire trail checkout --trail ` switches the checkout, and `--worktree` puts it under `.entire/worktrees` instead — useful when the main checkout is already on the base branch. ### 4. Do the work Work on the branch and commit normally. **Checkpoints capture the AI session automatically** — don't create checkpoints by hand unless the user asks. `entire status` shows sync state; a checkpoint reaches origin with the next `git push origin`. `entire checkpoint list` shows what has been captured. ### 5. Post findings Findings are how review feedback reaches the work. Post them against the change, with the file and line that the finding is about: ```sh entire trail finding add --trail \ --file lib/event_aggregation_pipeline.py --line 50 \ --severity medium -m "What is wrong and why it matters" ``` `--confidence` takes 0.0–1.0, and `--patch` / `--patch-file` attach a suggested diff (it must modify a single existing file in the worktree). Findings are for feedback. Comments (`entire trail comment`) are for people — post review feedback as a finding, not a comment. ### 6. Report Give the user the full URLs of the trail and the change, what was done, and what is still outstanding. Include the URL whenever you reference a trail or change so they can click through. ## Guardrails - `entire trail` commands need network access and the OS keychain. If you hit "Keychain is not accessible" or a network error, that is the sandbox, not a logged-out state: ask to re-run it unsandboxed. Do not run `entire login`. - `enable`, `disable`, `clean`, `auth`, `login`, and `logout` are the user's to run — suggest them, don't run them. - Writing intent onto a shared trail is outward-facing. Confirm the title and body with the user before writing, and confirm before creating a trail. - If it's unclear whether work belongs on an existing trail or a new one, ask rather than picking for them. ## Quick reference | Task | Command | | --- | --- | | List trails | `entire trail list --project /` | | Inspect a trail | `entire trail show

--project / --json` | | Set intent | `entire trail update

--title "..." --body "..."` | | New trail + branch | `entire trail create ... --branch-action=create --base main` | | Attach existing branch | `entire trail link

--branch --base main` | | Get onto a change | `entire trail checkout --trail [--worktree]` | | Post a finding | `entire trail finding add --trail --file -m "..."` | | Checkpoints | `entire checkpoint list` / `entire status` | ARGUMENTS: let's make sure we have appropriate quality control guards to this repository

"""Real-time speech-to-text pipeline built on the Moonshine streaming transcriber."""

import os
import queue

import numpy as np
from moonshine_voice import ModelArch, Transcriber, TranscriptEventListener

from lib.audio_pipeline import AudioPipelineConfig
from lib.segments import ASRSegmentEvent


class MoonshineRealTimePipeline:
    """Streams microphone blocks through Moonshine and emits ASR segment events.

    Requires the MOONSHINE_MODEL_PATH environment variable to point at a
    downloaded Moonshine model (see README). Only float32 audio is supported.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        input_audio_queue: queue.Queue,
        audio_pipeline_config: AudioPipelineConfig,
        output_event_queue: queue.Queue,
    ):
        # TODO: use input audio queue and audio pipeline config
        self.input_audio_queue = input_audio_queue
        self.output_event_queue = output_event_queue
        self.model_path = os.environ["MOONSHINE_MODEL_PATH"]
        self.model_arch = ModelArch.MEDIUM_STREAMING
        self.audio_pipeline_config = audio_pipeline_config

        if audio_pipeline_config.dtype != "float32":
            raise ValueError(
                f"Moonshine pipeline does not support this dtype: {audio_pipeline_config.dtype}"
            )

        self.transcriber = Transcriber(
            model_path=self.model_path,
            model_arch=self.model_arch,
        )
        self.transcriber.add_listener(ASRListener(self.output_event_queue))

    def run_loop(self):
        """Feed queued audio blocks into the transcriber until the process exits."""
        self.transcriber.start()
        print("Moonshine Ready")
        print("*" * 50)
        try:
            while True:
                audio_block = self.input_audio_queue.get()
                self.transcriber.add_audio(
                    np.asarray(audio_block, dtype=np.float32),
                    self.audio_pipeline_config.sample_rate,
                )
        finally:
            self.transcriber.stop()

    @classmethod
    def start_moonshine(
        cls,
        input_audio_queue: queue.Queue,
        audio_pipeline_config: AudioPipelineConfig,
        output_event_queue: queue.Queue,
    ):
        """Starts ASR pipeline."""
        MoonshineRealTimePipeline(
            input_audio_queue=input_audio_queue,
            audio_pipeline_config=audio_pipeline_config,
            output_event_queue=output_event_queue,
        ).run_loop()


class ASRListener(TranscriptEventListener):
    """Converts completed Moonshine transcript lines into ASRSegmentEvents."""

    def __init__(self, output_event_queue: queue.Queue):
        super().__init__()
        self.output_event_queue = output_event_queue

    def on_line_completed(self, event):
        """Publish an ASRSegmentEvent for each finalized transcript line."""
        line = event.line

        event = ASRSegmentEvent(
            start=line.start_time,
            end=line.start_time + line.duration,
            text=line.text,
        )
        self.output_event_queue.put(event.as_dict())

import os

import httpx


class OpenRouterProvider:
    """Calls an OpenRouter chat model with a messages list and returns the reply text."""

    def __init__(self, model: str, max_tokens: int, timeout: float):
        self.model = model
        self.max_tokens = max_tokens
        self.timeout = timeout

    def generate(
        self,
        messages_prompt: list,
        session_id: str,
    ) -> str:
        """Generate one completion for the given messages.

        Raises ValueError if OPENROUTER_API_KEY is unset, the request fails,
        or the response contains no text.
        """
        api_key = REDACTED
        if not api_key:
            raise ValueError(
                "Set OPENROUTER_API_KEY in your environment before calling OpenRouter."
            )

        status_code = None
        text = None
        try:
            with httpx.Client(timeout=self.timeout) as client:
                response = client.post(
                    "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions",
                    headers={
                        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                        "X-Session-Id": session_id,
                        "X-OpenRouter-Cache": "true",
                    },
                    json={
                        "model": self.model,
                        "messages": messages_prompt,
                        "max_tokens": self.max_tokens,
                        "temperature": 0.5,
                        "stream": False,
                    },
                )
                status_code = response.status_code
                text = response.text
                response.raise_for_status()

        except Exception as excp:
            raise ValueError(
                f"HTTP REQUEST FAILED (code: {status_code}): {text}"
            ) from excp

        payload = response.json()
        text = payload["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
        if not text:
            raise ValueError(f"Empty text in {payload}")
        return text

"""Client entrypoint: wires the real-time audio pipelines together as processes.

Spawns one process per stage — microphone capture, diarization (Nemotron),
ASR (Moonshine), event aggregation, and the API sink that forwards
aggregated transcription events to the server in `main.py`.
"""

import multiprocessing as mp

from lib.api_pipeline import ApiPipeline
from lib.audio_pipeline import AudioPipeline, AudioPipelineConfig
from lib.event_aggregation_pipeline import EventAggregationPipeline
from lib.moonshine_pipeline import MoonshineRealTimePipeline
from lib.nemotron_pipeline import NemotronRealTimePipeline

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Create base queues for inter-process communication
    mp.set_start_method("spawn")

    event_queue = mp.Queue()
    aggregated_event_queue = mp.Queue()
    nemotron_audio_queue = mp.Queue()
    moonshine_audio_queue = mp.Queue()

    # Create processes
    audio_pipeline_config = AudioPipelineConfig()  # use default values
    audio_pipeline_process = mp.Process(
        target=AudioPipeline.start_audio_pipeline,
        args=(
            [nemotron_audio_queue, moonshine_audio_queue],
            audio_pipeline_config,
        ),
    )
    nemotron_process = mp.Process(
        target=NemotronRealTimePipeline.start_nemotron,
        args=(
            nemotron_audio_queue,
            audio_pipeline_config,
            event_queue,
        ),
    )
    moonshine_process = mp.Process(
        target=MoonshineRealTimePipeline.start_moonshine,
        args=(
            moonshine_audio_queue,
            audio_pipeline_config,
            event_queue,
        ),
    )
    event_aggregation_process = mp.Process(
        target=EventAggregationPipeline.start_event_aggregation,
        args=(
            event_queue,
            aggregated_event_queue,
        ),
    )
    api_process = mp.Process(
        target=ApiPipeline.start_api_sync, args=(aggregated_event_queue,)
    )
    created_processes = [
        ("audio_pipeline", audio_pipeline_process),
        ("nemotron", nemotron_process),
        ("moonshine", moonshine_process),
        ("event_aggregation", event_aggregation_process),
        ("api_process", api_process),
    ]

    # Start processes
    for name, p in created_processes:
        p.start()

    # TODO: implement stop event handling
    keep_running = True
    while keep_running:
        for p_name, p in created_processes:
            if not p.is_alive():
                print(f"process {p} died")
                keep_running = False

"""OpenRouter's chat-completions API, via the existing HTTP dependency."""

import os

import httpx


class OpenRouterProvider:
    """Calls an OpenRouter chat model with a messages list and returns the reply text."""

    def __init__(self, model: str, max_tokens: int, timeout: float):
        self.model = model
        self.max_tokens = max_tokens
        self.timeout = timeout

    def generate(
        self,
        messages_prompt: list,
        session_id: str,
    ) -> str:
        """Generate one completion for the given messages.

        Raises ValueError if OPENROUTER_API_KEY is unset, the request fails,
        or the response contains no text.
        """
        api_key = REDACTED
        if not api_key:
            raise ValueError(
                "Set OPENROUTER_API_KEY in your environment before calling OpenRouter."
            )

        status_code = None
        text = None
        try:
            with httpx.Client(timeout=self.timeout) as client:
                response = client.post(
                    "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/chat/completions",
                    headers={
                        "Authorization": f"Bearer {api_key}",
                        "X-Session-Id": session_id,
                        "X-OpenRouter-Cache": "true",
                    },
                    json={
                        "model": self.model,
                        "messages": messages_prompt,
                        "max_tokens": self.max_tokens,
                        "temperature": 0.5,
                        "stream": False,
                    },
                )
                status_code = response.status_code
                text = response.text
                response.raise_for_status()

        except Exception as excp:
            raise ValueError(
                f"HTTP REQUEST FAILED (code: {status_code}): {text}"
            ) from excp

        payload = response.json()
        text = payload["choices"][0]["message"]["content"]
        if not text:
            raise ValueError(f"Empty text in {payload}")
        return text

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Regenerate qc/audit-baseline.txt from the current uv.lock.
#
# Run this after a dependency bump, then review the diff. Every newly added
# ID is an advisory that CI will now accept silently, so check each one for
# reachability from this project's code before committing the result.
set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

baseline="qc/audit-baseline.txt"
header_lines=13

tmp="$(mktemp -d)"
trap 'rm -rf "$tmp"' EXIT

# The text output lists exactly the advisory IDs uv reports, but it can list
# the same advisory twice under two ID schemes (a GHSA id and a PYSEC id).
# uv only matches one of them, so the candidate list is verified against uv
# itself below and any id uv rejects is dropped.
uv audit --preview-features audit-command >"$tmp/raw.txt" || true

grep -oE '^- (GHSA|PYSEC)-[0-9A-Za-z-]+:' "$tmp/raw.txt" \
  | sed -e 's/^- //' -e 's/:$//' \
  | sort -u >"$tmp/candidates.txt"

args=()
while read -r id; do
  [ -n "$id" ] && args+=(--ignore "$id")
done <"$tmp/candidates.txt"

# uv reports every id it could not match; drop those so CI stays quiet.
uv audit --preview-features audit-command "${args[@]}" >"$tmp/verify.txt" 2>&1 || true
grep -oE 'Ignored vulnerability `[A-Z]+-[0-9A-Za-z-]+` does not match' "$tmp/verify.txt" \
  | sed -e 's/Ignored vulnerability `//' -e 's/` does not match//' \
  | sort -u >"$tmp/unmatched.txt"

grep -vxF -f "$tmp/unmatched.txt" "$tmp/candidates.txt" >"$tmp/final.txt" || true

{
  head -"$header_lines" "$baseline"
  cat "$tmp/final.txt"
} >"$baseline.new"

mv "$baseline.new" "$baseline"

echo "Wrote $(grep -vc '^#' "$baseline") advisory IDs to $baseline"
if [ -s "$tmp/unmatched.txt" ]; then
  echo "Dropped $(wc -l <"$tmp/unmatched.txt" | tr -d ' ') id(s) uv does not match"
fi

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Regenerate qc/audit-baseline.txt from the current uv.lock.
#
# Run this after a dependency bump, then review the diff. Every newly added
# ID is an advisory that CI will now accept silently, so check each one for
# reachability from this project's code before committing the result.
set -euo pipefail

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

baseline="qc/audit-baseline.txt"
header_lines=13

tmp="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$tmp"' EXIT

# The text output lists exactly the advisory IDs that uv matches --ignore
# against. The JSON output also carries alias entries (the same advisory
# under a second ID scheme), and passing those produces a "does not match"
# warning on every run.
uv audit --preview-features audit-command >"$tmp" || true

ids="$(grep -oE '^- (GHSA|PYSEC)-[0-9A-Za-z-]+:' "$tmp" \
  | sed -e 's/^- //' -e 's/:$//' \
  | sort -u)"

{
  head -"$header_lines" "$baseline"
  printf '%s\n' "$ids"
} >"$baseline.new"

mv "$baseline.new" "$baseline"

echo "Wrote $(grep -vc '^#' "$baseline") advisory IDs to $baseline"

# helper

A local voice assistant. It listens to your microphone, works out who is
speaking, sends the utterance to an LLM, and speaks the reply back through
your speakers.

Everything runs on your machine except the LLM call, which goes to
[OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai).

## How it works

1. Your microphone is captured continuously in small blocks.
2. Two models read that audio in parallel: a **diarizer** decides *who* is
   talking, and a **transcriber** decides *what* was said.
3. A third stage joins the two by time overlap, so every transcript is
   attributed to a speaker.
4. The attributed text is POSTed to a local server that keeps the chat
   history, asks the LLM for a reply, and synthesizes that reply into audio.
5. The audio is played back on your speakers.

Because the assistant's own voice comes back through the microphone, the
server refuses events from the agent's speaker slot so it doesn't answer
itself.

## Architecture

Two entry points, run in separate processes.

### `client.py` — capture and understanding

Spawns one process per stage and connects them with multiprocessing queues.

```
                     ┌─► nemotron (diarization) ─┐
mic ─► audio_pipeline│                            ├─► event_aggregation ─► api_pipeline ─► POST /
                     └─► moonshine (ASR) ──────────┘
```

| Stage | Module | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capture | `lib/audio_pipeline.py` | Opens the mic with `sounddevice` and copies each 1600-sample block (16 kHz, mono, float32) into two queues. |
| Diarization | `lib/nemotron_pipeline.py` | Runs `nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization` in ultra-low-latency streaming mode over one queue and emits speaker segment events (`open` / `closed`). The model's speaker cache is carried across chunks so speakers stay consistent. |
| ASR | `lib/moonshine_pipeline.py` | Runs the Moonshine streaming transcriber over the other queue and emits transcript lines with start/end timestamps. |
| Aggregation | `lib/event_aggregation_pipeline.py` | Attributes each transcript to the speaker segment it overlaps most, producing `{text, speaker}` events. |
| Forwarding | `lib/api_pipeline.py` | POSTs each aggregated event to the assistant server. |

The event types exchanged between stages are defined in `lib/segments.py`.
All of them serialize to plain dicts so they can cross process queues;
timestamps are seconds relative to the start of the audio stream.

### `main.py` — the assistant

A FastAPI app that owns the session's chat history, calls OpenRouter for a
reply, and speaks it with Kokoro.

- **Model**: `google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite`, `max_tokens` 150, 5 s timeout,
  temperature 0.5.
- **Voice**: Kokoro TTS, `lang_code="a"` (American English), voice `af_heart`,
  24 kHz output.
- **Playback**: `sounddevice` writes to CoreAudio; the HTTP response returns
  as soon as playback is queued, not when the audio finishes.
- **Prompt**: the system prompt keeps replies to a single short sentence and
  tells the model to ask the user to repeat anything the transcription mangles,
  rather than guess.

## HTTP API

`POST http://127.0.0.1:8000/`

Request:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "transcription": "what is the weather like today",
    "speaker": 0
  }
}
```

Response (`200`):

```json
{
  "chat": [
    { "role": "system", "content": "You're an AI assistant. ..." },
    { "role": "user", "content": "what is the weather like today" },
    { "role": "assistant", "content": "It is sunny and warm." }
  ]
}
```

| Status | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `200` | Reply generated and queued for playback. The body is the full chat history. |
| `400` | `speaker` was missing, or the event came from the agent itself. |
| `500` | TTS produced no audio. |

## Setup

### 1. Python 3.12 (pyenv)

This project requires Python 3.12 (`requires-python = ">=3.12, <3.13"`). The
exact version is pinned in `.python-version`, so pyenv and uv agree on it.

```sh
brew install pyenv
pyenv install            # builds the version pinned in .python-version
pyenv global 3.12.9      # optional: default interpreter outside this repo
```

Put the shims on `PATH` in `~/.zshenv` (every shell) and initialise pyenv in
`~/.zshrc` (interactive shells):

```sh
export PYENV_ROOT="$HOME/.pyenv"
export PATH="$PYENV_ROOT/shims:$PATH"
eval "$(pyenv init -)"
```

`[tool.uv]` in `pyproject.toml` pins uv to the pyenv interpreter
(`python-preference = "only-system"`, `python-downloads = "never"`), so uv never
silently downloads a second, unpinned Python.

### 2. Dependencies

Install [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/), then:

```sh
uv sync
```

### 3. TLS roots

`certifi` and `virtualenv` are pinned at versions carrying the fix for the
October 2026 eMudhra/emSign CA incident
(<https://discuss.python.org/t/information-for-python-users-regarding-emudhra-emsign-ca-certificate-security-incident/109576>).
Keep `pip >= 26.2.2` and `certifi >= 2026.10.19` in any environment you create
outside uv.

### 4. Models and assets

Only one model has to be fetched by hand. The other two are pulled
automatically from Hugging Face the first time they run.

| Asset | How it is obtained |
| --- | --- |
| Moonshine STT model | Downloaded explicitly — see below. |
| `nvidia/Nemotron-3-Diarization` | Downloaded by `transformers` on the first run of the diarization stage. |
| Kokoro voices (`hexgrad/Kokoro-82M`) | Downloaded by `kokoro` the first time the voice is synthesised. |

Download the Moonshine transcription model:

```sh
uv run moonshine-voice download --stt --language en
```

The command prints a `Downloaded model path:` line. Copy that path — the
client needs it at runtime.

### 5. Environment variables

| Variable | Needed by | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | `main.py` | API key for the OpenRouter chat-completions call. The server raises `ValueError` on the first request if it is missing. |
| `MOONSHINE_MODEL_PATH` | `client.py` | Path to the downloaded Moonshine model. Read with `os.environ[...]`, so the client fails to start if it is missing. |

## Running

Two terminals.

**Terminal 1 — the assistant server:**

```sh
export OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...
uv run fastapi run main.py
```

It serves on `http://0.0.0.0:8000`. The client is hard-wired to
`http://127.0.0.1:8000` (`ApiConfig` in `lib/api_sdk.py`).

**Terminal 2 — the client pipelines:**

```sh
export MOONSHINE_MODEL_PATH=/path/to/downloaded/model
uv run python client.py
```

Speak, and the assistant answers out loud. On macOS the first run will ask for
microphone access.

To keep secrets out of your shell history, put them in a `.env` file (it is
git-ignored) and start the server with:

```sh
uv run uvicorn main:app --env-file .env
```

Note that `fastapi run` does **not** load `.env` on its own — only the
`--env-file` flag does.

## Configuration

The knobs currently live as module-level constants in `main.py`:

| Constant | Value | What it controls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `MODEL` | `google/gemini-2.5-flash-lite` | The chat model. |
| `MAX_TOKENS` | `150` | Hard cap on the reply length. |
| `TIMEOUT` | `5` | OpenRouter request timeout, in seconds. |
| `VOICE` | `af_heart` | Kokoro voice. |
| `LANG_CODE` | `a` | Kokoro language (American English). |
| `SAMPLE_RATE` | `24000` | Playback sample rate. |
| `AGENT_SPEAKER` | `1` | Speaker slot treated as the agent, and therefore ignored. |

The client-side capture settings live in `AudioPipelineConfig`
(`lib/audio_pipeline.py`): 16 kHz, mono, float32, 1600-sample blocks.

## Development

```sh
uv run pytest                                     # tests
uv run pytest --cov=lib --cov-report=term-missing # with coverage
uv run ruff check . && uv run ruff format .       # lint and format
uv run pre-commit run --all-files                 # pre-commit hooks
```

Tests currently cover the segment overlap math and the event aggregation
pipeline (`tests/test_event_aggregation_pipeline.py`).

## Known limitations

- **The chat history is a single in-memory list.** The server keeps the session's
  messages in a module-level `Chat` object (`global_chat` in `main.py`, backed
  by `lib/chat.py`), shared by every speaker, and it is lost whenever the
  server restarts. There is no persistence layer yet.
- **Aggregation can drop a transcript.** The aggregation stage flushes all
  pending ASR and diarization segments as soon as it publishes one aggregated
  event, so a transcript whose speaker segment has not closed yet can be
  discarded along with it. The code also assumes ASR events always arrive
  after diarization events for the same span — watermarking would be the fix
  for out-of-order arrival.
- **The loop guard depends on speaker numbering.** Diarizer slots are numbered
  in order of first arrival, so `AGENT_SPEAKER = 1` means "the second speaker
  to talk". The assistant only stops answering itself if it happens to take
  that slot.
- **No graceful shutdown in the client.** `client.py` has a TODO for stop-event
  handling, and because the stage processes are spawned rather than daemonic,
  stopping the client can leave them running.
- **No tool calling.** The model can only answer with text.

## Roadmap

| # | Item | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | Smooth ASR | Done — Moonshine streaming transcriber. |
| 1 | Decision layer | Done — OpenRouter completion over the session chat history, spoken with Kokoro. |
| 2 | Tool calling layer | Not started. |
| 3 | Memory persistence | Not started. |

      - name: Import every module
        run: |

          import importlib
          import pkgutil

          import lib

          failures = []
          for module in pkgutil.iter_modules(lib.__path__):
              name = f"lib.{module.name}"
              try:
                  importlib.import_module(name)
              except Exception as exc:
                  failures.append(f"{name}: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")

          if failures:
              raise SystemExit("import failures:\n" + "\n".join(failures))
          print("all lib modules import cleanly")
          PY

on:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

# The project's pyproject.toml pins uv to a pyenv-managed interpreter
# (python-preference = "only-system", python-downloads = "never") so a local
# checkout never silently runs a second, unpinned Python. CI wants the
# opposite: a reproducible interpreter it controls. These overrides apply to
# the workflow only and never touch the developer's machine.
env:
  UV_PYTHON_DOWNLOADS: automatic
  UV_PYTHON_PREFERENCE: only-managed

jobs:
  lint:
    name: Lint
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Install dev tooling
        run: uv sync --only-group dev
      - name: ruff check
        run: uv run --no-sync ruff check .
      - name: ruff format
        run: uv run --no-sync ruff format --check .

  test:
    name: Test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"
      # The tests import nothing beyond the standard library and pytest, so
      # this job deliberately installs only the dev group. It stays in the
      # low seconds instead of pulling the multi-gigabyte torch/nemo stack.
      - name: Install dev tooling
        run: uv sync --only-group dev
      - name: pytest
        run: uv run --no-sync pytest

  audit:
    name: Dependency audit
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
          # No install step: uv audit reads uv.lock directly.
      - name: Audit dependencies against the recorded baseline
        run: |
          args=()
          while read -r id; do
            case "$id" in ''|\#*) continue ;; esac
            args+=(--ignore "$id")
          done < qc/audit-baseline.txt
          uv audit --preview-features audit-command "${args[@]}"

  docs:
    name: Docs
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: "22"
      - name: markdownlint
        run: npx --yes markdownlint-cli2@0.24.0

  smoke:
    name: Import smoke test (advisory)
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    # Advisory while it settles: the model and audio modules have no unit
    # tests, so importing them is the only check that the dependency tree
    # still resolves. Flip this to blocking once the install has proved
    # reliable on the runner image.
    continue-on-error: true
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v5
        with:
          enable-cache: true
          python-version: "3.12"
      - name: Install full dependency set
        run: uv sync
      - name: Import every module
        run: |
          uv run --no-sync python - <<'PY'
          import importlib
          import pkgutil

          import lib

          failures = []
          for module in pkgutil.iter_modules(lib.__path__):
              name = f"lib.{module.name}"
              try:
                  importlib.import_module(name)
              except Exception as exc:
                  failures.append(f"{name}: {type(exc).__name__}: {exc}")

          if failures:
              raise SystemExit("import failures:\n" + "\n".join(failures))
          print("all lib modules import cleanly")
          PY

## Quality control

GitHub Actions runs on every push and pull request
(`.github/workflows/ci.yml`):

| Job | What it enforces |
| --- | --- |
| `lint` | `ruff check` and `ruff format --check`, against the rule set in `pyproject.toml`. |
| `hygiene` | No trailing whitespace, every file ends in a newline, no leftover merge conflict markers. |
| `test` | `pytest`, with a coverage floor that fails the build if coverage drops below it. |
| `audit` | `uv audit` against a recorded baseline of known advisories, so a new one fails the build. |
| `docs` | `markdownlint` over this README. |
| `smoke` | Advisory: imports every module against the full dependency set, catching dependency breakage the unit tests cannot see. |

Two details worth knowing:

**The test job is fast because it installs almost nothing.** The tests import
only the standard library and pytest, so CI installs the dev dependency group
alone and never pulls the multi-gigabyte torch and nemo stack. The `smoke` job
is what exercises the full dependency set.

**The dependency audit is baselined, not clean.** `uv audit` currently reports
69 advisories, almost all in the transitive ML tree — 44 in `pillow`, 8 in
`nemo-toolkit`, 6 in `filelock`, 5 in `pytorch-lightning`. They are listed in
`qc/audit-baseline.txt` and ignored by CI, so the job passes today and fails
the moment a new advisory appears. Regenerate the baseline after a dependency
bump with:

```sh
./scripts/update-audit-baseline.sh
```

Review that diff carefully — every newly added ID is one CI will now accept
silently.

## Development

```sh
uv run pytest                    # tests
uv run ruff check .              # lint
uv run ruff format .             # format
uv run pre-commit run --all-files # pre-commit hooks
python3 scripts/check_hygiene.py # file hygiene
```

Configuration lives in `pyproject.toml`: the pytest `testpaths` and coverage
options, the coverage floor (`[tool.coverage.report] fail_under`), and the
ruff rule set.

Tests currently cover the segment overlap math and the event aggregation
pipeline (`tests/test_event_aggregation_pipeline.py`). The model, audio and
network paths are not unit tested — they need downloaded models and hardware,
so `smoke` covers them by import instead.
